Mr. President, We take note of UNDP's efforts to adapt under the UN 80 and constrained funding environment, including measures to improve efficiency and maximize development impact. Mr. President, we look forward to continuing.

This requires the timely and effective implementation of the Seville commitment, strengthen multilateral cooperation, fulfillment of official development assistance commitments, technology transfer and capacity building support, enhance access to concessional financing, debt sustainability measures and determination of unilateral coercive measures that undermine member states capacities to achieve sustainable development and constrain UNDP ability to effectively deliver its mandate on the ground. Mr. Administrator, as you rightly acknowledged today, developing countries are making significant efforts to invest their own national budgets through UNDP, with government development financing reaching nearly $1.6 billion in 2025 and now representing 29% of UNDP's total contributions. Bearing in mind that public resources are already under increasing pressure and that international financing required to achieve national development priorities and the sustainable development goals goes far beyond what traditional aid alone is delivering in the current political context, the Group of 77 and China appreciates your commitment to advancing a new model of development partnerships that strengthens South-South cooperation and mobilizes the private sector as strategic partner for development, including through initiatives such as the UNDP flagship investment accelerator and the SDG investor maps. Amid a challenging development landscape and the multiple global crises we are currently facing, The Group of 77 and China wishes to reaffirm its full support for you and your efforts to adapt and strengthen the development system based on national ownership, creative international partnerships, and renewed trust through greater coordination and cost efficiencies, as well as measurable results and deliverables for member states. I thank you.
I thank Uruguay for the statement on behalf of the G77 and China. I give the floor to Nepal to be on behalf of the LDC group to be followed by the Philippines. Nepal, please, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President, UNDP Administrator, dear colleagues. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the group of the least developed countries. The LDC group thanks the Administrator for his substantive remarks and expresses its appreciation to UNDP for its continued commitment to supporting the cause of the LDCs. We recognize that UNDP's strategic plan 2026-2029 that focuses on prosperity for all, effective governance, crisis resilience, and a healthy planet underpinned by digital transformation, gender equality, and sustainable finance is closely aligned with the priorities and development realities of the LDCs. The LDC Group reaffirms that the special needs and priorities of LDCs must remain at the center of UNDP programming. financing, policy support, and capacity building efforts. We acknowledge that UNDP continues to play a unique role in LDCs through its country presence, policy expertise, and operational support. Beyond program delivery, it has helped strengthen institutions, mobilize partnership, and support integrated solutions to complex development challenges. The group remains concerned by the continued decline in development financing and the pressure on flexible and core resources. We are particularly concerned that these trends could weaken support at a time when LDCs require greater assistance to accelerate recovery, build resilience, and advance structural transformation. We therefore encourage UNDP to safeguard its country-level capacity and continue providing integrated, country-driven support aligned with national priorities and cooperation frameworks. In this context, Mr. President, the group would like to underscore the following points. First, we encourage UNDP to further strengthen support for the implementation of the Doha Program of Action. The upcoming DPUA midterm review in Doha next year presents an important opportunity to accelerate progress, address persistent implementation gaps, and mobilize renewed international support for LDCs. We stress continued alignment of country programs and financing strategies with DPUA priorities. Second, productive capacity development, economic transformation, and sustainable graduation must remain at the forefront of UNDP support. LDCs require enhanced assistance for infrastructure development, energy access, digital transformation, trade capacity, value addition, and institution building. These investments are essential to ensuring sustainable growth, employment creation, and successful graduation pathways. Third, we welcome UNDP's strong emphasis on resilience building and crisis prevention. For LDCs, development is the first line of defense against instability and vulnerability. We therefore call for expanded support for climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, early warning systems, and locally led resilience building. Fourth, we encourage UNDP to deepen its support for sustainable finance, domestic resource mobilization, and debt sensitive development planning. Many LDCs face shrinking fiscal space and rising debt service burdens that constrain investment in development priorities. Extend and support in this. areas remains critical. Finally, we underline the importance of digital transformation and robust data systems. Investment in digital public infrastructure, connectivity, statistical capacity, and digital skills can help LDCs accelerate development and improve public service delivery. Such efforts should contribute to narrowing rather than widening existing digital divides. In closing, Mr. President, predictable and flexible funding remains essential for effective development cooperation. We therefore reiterate the importance of regular resources in enabling UNDP to deliver integrated, impartial and country-driven support, particularly in countries furthest behind. The LDC Group also reiterates its support for ongoing efforts to enhance efficiency, effectiveness and coherence across the United Nations development system. We underscore that reforms must extend and not diminish development capacity in programme countries, and efficiency gains should translate into stronger country support, improved expertise and better development outcomes on the ground. In this regard, we would welcome hearing from the Administrator how UNDP intends to implement its strategic plan in LDCs under current financing constraints, while ensuring that reforms continue to support country level delivery, DPOA implementation and sustainable graduation efforts. The LDC Group looks forward to continuing its partnership with UNDP, including in the lead up to DPOA midterm review to advance sustainable development and ensure that no LDC is left behind. And in my national capacity, I just wish to add a word of appreciation and gratitude to UNDP administrator for the kind message of sympathy and solidarity as you face it another devastating natural calamity. And so far, 16 people have been reported dead and over Around 400 people are reported missing, among which 291 are foreign nationals. So we, the people in Nepal, are confident that with the support and solidarity of the international community and our national efforts,

we will be able to overcome this tragedy. Indeed, our condolences as well. We are seeing the news coming from Nepal, the floods affecting and killing for the time being 72 already. civilians, which is very tragic. So please accept our condolences and compassion. I also want to thank you for the statement that you delivered on behalf of the LDCs. And we continue with the Philippines on behalf of the like-minded group. And then we will be hearing from Cuba, Germany, India, Rwanda, Cote d'Ivoire. give the floor to the Philippines on behalf of the like-minded group for middle-income countries.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Condolences and sympathies also to the government and people of Nepal. Administrator De Croo, Excellencies, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the like-minded group for middle-income countries composed of Armenia, Belarus, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Lebanon, Mexico, Morocco, Namibia, Panama, Peru, Uruguay, and my country, the Philippines. The group welcomes this interactive dialogue as an affirmation of UNDP's commitment to deliver on the development agenda on the ground and advancing nationally led sustainable development efforts across middle income countries. The LMG mix reassures UNDP of its partnership in ensuring that development remains, as the Administrator mentioned, at the center of global decision-making, and that the UN development system continues to deliver results amidst the many challenges that have put strains on multilateralism. As reaffirmed in the Makati Declaration, the repositioned UN development system continues to play an important role in supporting the development pathways and transitions of middle income countries. We count on UN country teams, including the UNDP, to leverage their convening power, partnerships, and expertise to help sustain development gains, address structural vulnerabilities, and accelerate progress towards the sustainable development goals. In this regard, the group continues to advance two key priorities. First, the development of a comprehensive system-wide response plan for middle-income countries, and secondly, the elaboration of a strategic plan of action for MICs. The LMG MICs welcomes UNDP's efforts to advance the UNAD initiative as an opportunity to strengthen a more integrated, responsive, and country-driven UN development system, one that is better equipped to support countries' diverse development pathways. Against this backdrop, allow me to emphasize the following points. First, we must ensure that country configurations remain responsive to the evolving realities and specific needs of middle-income countries and avoid one-size-fits-all approaches. We support continued work as mandated by resolution 72/279 towards transparent and objective criteria developed in consultation with host governments that respond to national priorities, capacities and development context. Second, rationalization should not result in standardized approaches that may affect country engagement and governments access to UN entities on the ground. We stress that national ownership must remain the cornerstone of future UN country configurations. Third, UNAD should contribute to a more balanced and sustainable funding architecture that enables the UN development system to respond to specific challenges faced by middle income countries. We therefore support a healthy funding mix built upon a strong core funding base and complemented by thematic pooled and flexible earmarked resources, each serving distinct and complementary purposes. Fourth, We expect that UN country teams and the UNDP remain focused on enabling access to concessional financing, innovative and green technologies, renewable energy, infrastructure, climate action, and digital transformation. We underscore, as also the administrator mentioned this morning, the catalytic role of South-South and triangular cooperation in advancing these priorities. Lastly, Mr. President, the UNDP's wide and far-reaching country presence, policy expertise and long-standing partnerships with our governments place it in a unique and special position to support implementation of nationally owned development goals. We therefore count on the UNDP's continued support in advancing work towards elaboration of a strategic plan of action for middle income countries. I thank you, Mr. President.

And as a consequence, the logistical supply chain that sustains cooperation with the programme. As a result of this, a dozen UNDP containers are being held in ports across the region. President, First of all, let me join others in expressing my solidarity with Nepal and condolences to the victims and their families. Administrator Decroo, dear Alexander, thank you very much for this interactive dialogue and for laying out in your remarks how UNDP is adapting to its model, its development model to a difficult and getting more difficult financing environment. We need reforms, you know that. We support UNAT, which encompasses the UN funds and programs as well, and we need reforms in challenging times and multifaceted pressures. Let me make a few points and a few questions we have as well. We share your concern about the continued decline in core resources. Maintaining overall revenue through earmarked and government co-financing cannot substitute for predictable core funding. Core resources are essential for UNDP's integrator role for accountability and oversight and for acting early in crises. And that's why Germany increased its core contribution despite severe budget constraints. Secondly, we welcome the positive MOPAN assessment, but at the same time, MOPAN points to the need for further strength and performance and results-based management. And I would be grateful if you could elaborate a little bit how UNDP will use these findings to demonstrate measurable results more systematically. Thirdly, we welcome your emphasis on early recovery and development from day one in crisis settings. In this spirit, Germany is preparing a contribution of 10 million euros to the UN Palestine Recovery Trust Fund. We see the fund as part of broader support for the United Nations critical role in the Palestinian territory for the implementation of Security Council Resolution 2803 and the peace plan for Gaza and as part of the new Team Europe initiative for early recovery of Gaza. So if you could explain a little bit on that point, we would appreciate it. Mr. President, we thank Administrator Decroo for his comprehensive statement. We acknowledge the outstanding contributions of ASG Ahuna and ASG Kani Vignarajah as they leave UNDP after years of dedicated service. Thank you very much for all you have done for our region. The administrator has ably outlined today's operational environment for UNDP. India commends UNDP's efforts to align its structures, footprint, workforce and operating model to today's realities. India maintains that the development pillar must remain the top priority under the UNAD initiative with a continued focus on strengthening support to countries of the global south. However, we must not try to fix something that isn't broke. We thank you, Mr. President, for your leadership on this account and for leading the board and all members in discussing the UNAD initiative and its impact on UNDP. India has been a strong advocate for promoting investments in livelihoods, institutions, infrastructure, education, healthcare, and social protection through its various domestic initiatives. We collaborate closely with UNDP as we take some of these experiences to friends and partners in the global south. India advocates for a more holistic, inclusive and sustainable economic growth model with emphasis on national ownership and country-led development pathways. We appreciate UNDP's growing engagement with governments as co-investors in their own development, reflected in the rise of government development financing. India also maintains that solutions cannot be dictated from outside. Instead, they must be introduced by Member States and driven by their national priorities, capacities and circumstances. Mr. President, India values its close collaboration with UNDP in operationalizing the India UN Development Partnership Fund and the India Brazil South Africa Fund, the IBSA Fund. Through these two funds, we have committed over $150 million to advance digital infrastructure, health, and climate resilience with special focus on LDCs and SIDS. This reflects South-South cooperation, which as Administrator noted, is a new model of partnership, one that enables developing countries to share knowledge, connect capabilities, mobilize more of their own resources, and access capital on better terms. We also note the problem of funding and the sharp decline in core funding to the UN development system as a whole. We reaffirm that India is a consistent core contributor to UNDP and encourage other partners to contribute through domestic public resources and strengthen the core funding, enabling UNDP to act early, innovate and deliver at scale. In conclusion, we reaffirm our commitment to multilateral cooperation and look forward to working constructively with UNDP, the UNFPA, and the UNOPS in advancing the 2030 agenda. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank India for the statement. I give the floor to Rwanda, to be followed by Cote d'Ivoire, Nauru, Sweden, Bangladesh. Rwanda, please, Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President and Mr. Administrator. I join you and colleagues to express our condolences to the government and the people of Nepal. One aligns itself with the statements delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China and the LDC group. And the African group wishes to offer the following remarks in its national capacity. We thank the UNDP administrator for his statement and for his leadership of UNDP and at a particular consequential moment for international development cooperation. Mr. President, Rwanda is concerned by the scale and speed of the contraction in development finance described before us. The figures are stark. Official development assistance declined by 23.1% in 2025, noted as the largest fall on record. During that same period, UNDP's core funding declined by 24%. These are not merely financial adjustments. They represent a significant hurt in the resources available to developing countries, precisely when financing needs, debt burdens, climate vulnerabilities, and development challenges are increasing. Equally concerning is the continued erosion of UNDP's core resources. Core funding now represents less than one-tenth of UNDP's overall resources, far below the ambitions set under the funding compact. For Rwanda, this raises a fundamental question about the development model we collectively expect UNDP to sustain. We expect UNDP to remain present in program countries, to respond rapidly in times of crisis, to provide impartial policy advice, to support national institutions, to innovate, to mobilize financing, and to serve as an integrator across the United Nations development system. Yet all these functions depend on predictable and flexible core resources. Against this backdrop, would the administrator see scope for non-core funding to contribute more effectively to sustaining essential core capacities? And if this is an area that could benefit from further engagements within the executive board. Mr. President, Rwanda recognizes the need for UNDP to remain efficient, agile, and financially disciplined. However, efficiency cannot substitute for adequate financing, nor can reform become a means of managing an ever-smaller development pillar. Rwanda remains committed to working with UNDP and fellow board members towards development system that is efficient, adequately resourced, responsive to national priorities, and capable of delivering at the scale that present moment, the present moment requires. I thank you.
I thank Rwanda for the statement. I give the floor to Cote d'Ivoire to be followed by Nauru. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you, President. We would like to join everyone in offering Nepal our condolences. My delegation associates itself to the statement of the African Group and we would like to add the following on a national basis. We would like to thank the Administrator for introducing his report and we note with satisfaction the fact that UNDP has mobilized $9.6 billion between 2022 and 2025, around 91% of estimated contributions as well as its growing support to countries when it comes to poverty reduction, governance, resiliency, climate and gender equality. We are nevertheless concerned by a drop of 24% in core resources in 2025, which is now limited to 9% of total contributions. While the needs of developing countries continue to be considerable and the SDGs are significantly behind, Cote d'Ivoire would like to reaffirm the need to have more predictable, multi-year and flexible resources, which would allow UNDP to respond to national and regional priorities as well as preserve its technical and institutional capacities and rapidly act. in a crisis. We would like to welcome the diversification of partnerships with IFIs, the private sector, philanthropists, as well as sustainable financing mechanisms. This diversification should complement without replacing core resources, which are indispensable for the neutrality, flexibility, and institutional capacity of the program. Cote d'Ivoire also welcomes the role that UNDP has played in UN system reform. comes to development and UNAD, this reform should be based on more consistent financing by reducing fragmentation and favoring common financing as well as integrated approaches in our countries. To conclude, President, Cote d'Ivoire reaffirms its full support to UNDP and we remain convinced that adequate and quality financing is critical in order to implement the strategic program 2026-2029 in order to accelerate SDGs. I thank you.

Like to thank Cote d'Ivoire for the statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of Nauru.

Mr. President, Mr. Administrator, dear colleagues, let me begin by expressing Sweden's appreciation for UNDP's continued delivery of strong development results in an increasingly challenging global environment. We commend the organization for its commitment to reform and recognize that maintaining long-term institutional capacity will become increasingly difficult if the decline in flexible and predictable funding continues. Sweden welcomes UNDP's efforts to adapt to a changing financial landscape and its strong focus on efficiency and cost effectiveness. In particular, Sweden would like to extend its gratitude to the staff transferred to new duty station as part of this effort. Sweden greatly appreciates the regular and harmonized structured funding dialogues and transparent reporting that accompanies. To maximize efficiency, we encourage UNDP to partner with us in consolidating fewer demand driven and high impact programs. excellencies as one of the country's most vulnerable to climate change Bangladesh highly values undp support in strengthening National capacities and advancing climate resilience we encourage undp to enhance technical assistance for accessing the green climate fund the global environment facility and loss and damage financing mechanisms we also look forward to expanded collaboration in coastal adaptation ecosystem restoration and sustainable River management Bangladesh remains fully committed to a smooth, sustainable and irreversible transition from the LDC category. I thank Bangladesh for the statement. I give the floor to the United States, to be followed by Brazil.

Good afternoon. We echo Administrator De Croo's candid observation in a recent interview that emphasizing aid is a matter of the past. and that development must be viewed through a logic of investment that mobilizes private capital. The United States Trade Over Aid Initiative is pivoting away from government to government dependency traps and prioritizes private sector partnerships that build lasting economic self-reliance. We thank UNDP for its work to establish business enabling environments by strengthening property rights, building legitimate legal systems, and making markets investable. Going forward, UNDP's success must be measured by self-reliance achieved and private capital unlocked. To fulfill this mission, UNDP must remain fiscally disciplined and fit for purpose. While recent reforms, such as deploying cloud-based enterprise resource planning systems, optimizing workforce structures, and consolidating back office functions, Aligned with the US priorities on administrative transparency, efficiency and cost containment, deeper changes are still urgently needed. The 2026 MOPAN assessment reveals an organization at the critical crossroads. Structurally, UNDP remains overly top heavy, maintaining a management tier of two under secretaries general and nine assistant secretaries general. despite the 71% real term collapse in core funding since 2011 and the removal of the resident coordinator system. This heavy executive architecture is financially unsustainable. UNDP must urgently restructure its executive leadership and downside top level overhead to reflect current fiscal realities. OPEN also correctly underscores that resource allocation formulas must be modernized. We must revise the methodology so core funding prioritizes low-income, fragile, and least developed countries where it is needed most. In alignment with broader UN-wide efficiency reforms, UNDP must immediately enforce spending controls and cease authorizing business class travel. Finally, UNDP must return to basics. On climate, UNDP must stay away from climate ideology and focus on environmental resilience and preparedness. On gender issues, stay away from ideology and focus on creating equal opportunity for men and women and boy and girls. And UNDP must favor opportunity for all and eliminate programs focused on diversity, equity, and inclusion. We look forward to working with the executive board and you, Administrator Decro, to deliver a leaner, high impact.
I thank the United States for the statement. I give the floor to Brazil to be followed by China.

Mr. President, Mr. Administrator, my delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the G77 in China, and we express our condolences to Nepal. President, at the outset, I thank Administrator DeCru for his introduction and for his reference to the flash flood occurring at the border of China and Nepal. China positively assesses the smooth implementation of UNDP's 10th country program with China and looks forward to seeing more early results. Second, UNDP should focus on addressing its funding challenges. China notes the significant decline in UNDP's core resources in 2025. The protection of these functions is vital to guarantee efficiency, transparency, and trust. Norway remains a staunch supporter of the UNDP as well as the funding compact. Mr. President, Excellencies, at the outset, Armenia would like to reaffirm its strong appreciation for UNDP's role as a central development partner. For Armenia, this role is particularly important. As a landlocked developing and middle-income country facing structural constraints, Armenia values development cooperation that is flexible, country-driven, and focused on long-term resilience and national capacity building. I thank Armenia for the statement. I give the floor to New Zealand and to be followed by the Dominican Republic.

Thank you, President. New Zealand also extends its sincere condolences to the government of Nepal and expresses our deepest sympathies to all those affected. Against this backdrop, and as you have said this morning, Administrator, we meet at a time when development gains are under sustained pressure. Conflict, climate change, and economic shocks are compounding, reversing progress, and increasing vulnerability. In this context, development remains fundamental to stability, resilience, and security, and must remain at the center of the UN's work. We therefore welcome UNDP's continued efforts to strengthen integrated system-wide responses and deliver impact at scale. New Zealand strongly supports the Secretary-General's UN 80 reform initiative as an opportunity to advance meaningful reform. We need a UN development system that is more focused, efficient and coordinated, and better able to deliver results for countries. We welcome UNDP's role as the integrator and operational backbone of the development system and encourage continued efforts to reduce duplication and direct resources towards delivery and results on the ground. We agree that increasingly complex development challenges cannot be addressed through fragmented and project-based approaches alone. As reform discussions progress, proposals should be assessed holistically, including reforms relating to UN country teams, the resident coordinator system, regional presence, and shared services. A strong resident coordinator system is essential to a more coherent and effective UN development system. However, strengthening coordination will require changes not only to structures, but also to incentives, accountability arrangements, reporting frameworks, and funding models that continue to drive fragmentation. As a Pacific country, New Zealand also emphasizes that presence matters. Geographic dispersion and capacity constraints mean that country and regional presence are operational requirements, not overhead costs. Reforms should preserve the UN's ability to deliver where it is needed most, while strengthening coordination with Pacific regional institutions and making better use of comparative advantages across the system. The recent MoPAN assessment provides valuable evidence for these discussions. We welcome its finding that UNDP is a strong and capable organization supported by robust operational systems, strong financial governance, and extensive country presence. At the same time, the assessment highlights ongoing challenges in achieving integrated strategic results, including incentives created by funding arrangements that favour fragmented project delivery. We encourage UNDP and member states to address these constraints as part of the broader reform agenda. In closing, New Zealand reaffirms its strong support for UNDP and its central roles in the development system. We look forward to working with partners to ensure that reforms under UNAT deliver a more coherent, efficient, accountable and country focused UNDS that strengthens national and regional institutions and delivers meaningful results for those most in need. Thank you.
I thank New Zealand for the statement. I'll give the floor to the Dominican Republic and then we will go to the administrator to address some of the comments. The Dominican Republic, please.

Thank you, President, Mr. Administrator, distinguished colleagues. We would like to thank the visionary intervention of the Administrator, and your words really resonate with our own experience and reflect the challenges that we face across the region. We fully agree. The development model is changing and financing for development must evolve from aid to investment. The unprecedented drop of official development assistance as well as core contributions to the UN system demands, as you rightfully said, to make sure that each development dollar works better. Mobilizing investments at a greater scale and reducing risks. In this sense, the Dr. has firmly moved towards a development project where the UNDP's technical cooperation has become a catalyzer for our own national investments. We do not see UNDP as an assistance provider, but rather a partner that provides technical intelligence and has the convening power necessary to make the most out of the resources that we mobilize. Allow me to share a specific example. Two months ago, in June of 2026, the Dominican Republic was recognized by UNDP as a regional example in democratic strengthening and poverty reduction. During the introduction of the Regional Report on Human Development 2026, the Regional Director for UNDP in Latin America and the Caribbean, Michel Musset, highlighted gains in our country in terms of consolidating electoral democracy and the strengthening of political freedoms. We are a relevant case of democratic strengthening in a moment where we see growing strain on That recognition is not a coincidence. And the response that we need is not whether the world needs a new development model, but whether we can allow ourselves not to build it. The Dominican Republic is committed to this project and we see UNDP as an important partner on this path that we are walking upon. I thank you.

I thank the Dominican Republic for the statement. We go to the administrator of the UNDP and then we come back with statements from Member States. We have Netherlands, Ukraine, Pakistan, El Salvador. Mr. Administrator.

Okay, we are halfway of the interventions, and I tried to group a bit the topics that have been covered. You remember that in my speech, I mentioned the importance of people and the sometimes difficult circumstance in which we work. And unfortunately, as a UN family, we have received bad news that there has been an incident in South Sudan where two peacekeepers from Ethiopia have been killed by an attack. Three from Ethiopia have been wounded and two from South Sudan have been injured as well. And really let us present our condolences to the families and hope that the ones who are injured can recover as soon as possible. Many interventions on funding obviously acknowledge, many of you have mentioned the importance of core funding and appreciate those who have called the increase of core funding. And we really understand, I think as UNDP, the difficult circumstances financial circumstances in which many of you are working. It's not only us who are in difficult financial circumstances. All of you are confronted with choices to be made. And our appeal really is to prioritize core. We understand that asking for more funding is difficult in these circumstances. So the real message is, if you cannot do more, please do core. and increase your core funding in the total, because the impact of core funding on the other projects is really huge one, and it helps us to mobilize other type of financing. And I think the intervention of Rwanda specifically talked about what it enables us to do. I mean, it enables the country presence that you have talked about. It enables our policy and our policy expertise. We know that the finances are tight and that working in our mandate is an important one. And as Zambia has mentioned, the name of the African states, our priority is development impact, right? We look at other types of financing, but always with the perspective of development impact. We might know that there might be other objectives. We're not against those other objectives, but our objective obviously is development impact. job creation, fighting the impact of climate change and so on. There have been questions on how does this impact the implementation of our strategic plan. Look, the impact of the core financing, 80% of the core financing that we have goes directly or indirectly to the implementation of our strategic plan. So if the core financing is being reduced, yes, it will have an impact. You know that one of the enablers in our strategic plan is gender. gender from an economic perspective, from the perspective of opportunity, from the perspective of potential and using the potential of the entirety of your population. We know that this topic is one which is on the funding side already being put under pressure. If CORE is also put under pressure, it makes it harder for us to fill those gaps. And so we should understand that the erosion of core has an impact on the priorities that you have put in our strategic plan and in climate mitigation programs and so on. I hope this is not a surprise for you. We have also had some questions on How can we diversify the funding? And I think in my introduction speech, I gave you many examples of how we look at diversifying, diversifying the funder base, diversifying the work that we do with international financial institutions, with private sector. These are questions asked by Cote d'Ivoire, by Finland, by Sweden, by Armenia. And I think we have been quite successful in doing that, but it's clear that we will have to multiply that, multiplying that. means getting our core funding work harder. And that was really the main line that I wanted to explain at the start of my speech, that core funding enables us to bring in other sources of financing. But of course, it's hard to bring in other sources of financing if we don't have a platform on which we can base it. So the access to core is the one that enables us to have access to other types of financing. Less core is also less access to other types of financing, which is financing which often is not ODA based, which is external to that. I have been questions on the MOPAN assessment. I think Germany, United States, New Zealand talked about that. I think Indeed, the MOPAN assessment showed how we have adapted and have become a stronger organisation. But MOPAN also talked about the fact that we have a business model which is very much focused on delivery and should be more focused on outcome. We agree with that, and in our interaction, we acknowledge that. But we also want to make one comment on that, is that one of the reasons why we are more delivery focused than outcome focused for the moment is because we have a high share of earmarked funding. If the funding is very earmarked on projects, obviously The reporting is very much on the delivery of those projects. If you want to go into a more impact perspective where we work with portfolios and integrated approach, we also need the funding to be able to do that. But we specifically in our interaction have mentioned that we are moving much more into the direction of portfolio. And I think also in the interactions with you, we will more and more in discussions on projects try to put it in a portfolio perspective. And go in an interaction with you, say, look, okay, interesting project, but from a portfolio perspective, it's probably better to rephrase the project in this way because it better fits the totality of what we want to do. Remarks on South-South by a number of countries. Maybe first of all address the point made by Brazil. Let's be very clear, we will deliver on the commitments that we have made and really in previous board meetings we have reassured you on this and let me do this again. We have a broad range of South-South vehicles, the Paris Giris Fund, the G77 and China Fund, the India Brazil South Africa Fund, which celebrates 20 years now, the India UN Fund, the UN China Fund. There's many, many of those funds in which we work. And we think this is one of the ways going forward is creating that South-South and triangular type of work. On the impact of cuts, I will get back on the impact of cuts. There's been questions by Rwanda, Norway, Nepal, name of the LDCs and Cote d'Ivoire on that. Specific questions were asked. the scope of how non-core can contribute to the erosion of core and helping the core capacity. We will look into different options along that track and try to look at it in a creative way. And some of you have suggested, well, maybe you can adapt your cost recovery and that cost recovery could compensate for the reduction in core. We're not against of looking into that direction, but you should know that if we want today to compensate for the erosion of core by increasing the cost recovery, that would mean that you would have to double the cost recovery. This could be part of the solution, but doubling cost recovery, I'm not sure this is the direction we want to go. So we're open to that discussion, but let's also be clear on how far you can actually go in doing that. And in any case, if we have that discussion, we need to do it in a harmonized way because the cost recovery rules are harmonized with UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women, and others. Let me then, there was a question on the middle income countries strategy asked by Philippines in name of the group of friends. I mean, we should not forget that two thirds of the world's poor, multidimensional poor are in that, in middle income countries. We are very active in middle income countries and obviously the type of work we do there is on financing for development, on preparing for digital, on diversifying economic growth, on job creation and it remains a high priority for us to continue working in that and we see that more and more. This is also evolving in the direction of government developed financing, which is a point which was made by Brazil. Yes, this is almost a third of the work that we do, work that we greatly appreciate. That has been growing quite a bit. It's grown 22% since 2022. To do that, we have strengthened and adapted our country presence, developing new skills, very often related to digital, to financial policy, and expertise linked to governance and so on. But it also calls for a shift in thinking on how we organize when this continues growing and also how do you organize the financial model around that? There was a remark made by Germany on the type of recovery and resilience work, for example, that we do in Gaza and in the occupied Palestinian territories. We greatly appreciate the partnership that we have. specifically in Gaza and occupied Palestinian territory, but in the broader region. And this is really crucial to work on resilience and to avoid that crisis would continue. We are also the main partner in the UN Palestinian Recovery Trust Fund and working really well together with other UN entities on doing that. On climate, and really, let me all reassure you, Neither for climate, neither for gender. This is based on ideology. This is based on economics. Our gender policy is based on economics. Because if you don't use the entirety of the talent that you have in your country, how can you develop the maximum potential of your country? And that's the same for our climate work. Our climate work today, it's economics. Throughout the world, we see that economic activity is slowing down. because of the impact of climate. This is not ideology, it's science. And scientists have told us years ago that this would come. So working our climate work is economic work. It's helping societies to adapt to new reality. It's part of security policy. We now have seen firsthand that energy strategy has a direct link to security. is a direct link to being less vulnerable. Economic vulnerability is today security vulnerability. And this is linked, of course, to the energy work that we do, mentioned by Cuba and its intervention. We have many examples of where we do this work, and I'm not going to get into detail in all the places where we do climate work. But climate and energy work is really work that we do for people. protecting people, it's supporting people very often in difficult circumstances. There was a remark on the small island development states by Nauru. As discussed in previous meetings, we have a big country presence and this is top of our agenda, is keeping our country presence in the small island development states, especially in the Pacific, but in general, keeping our country presence is very, very important. We have a presence in 36 of the of the of the sets and the range of work that we do is very broad, going from from from digital to green transmission, green transformation, but also to private capital. We have been able to launch a sovereign blue bond in in Fiji, which has raised 9 million euros. And we see that accessing that type of and financing works everywhere in the world, also in small island developing states. Talking about crisis, I think Spain and UK have mentioned that. Indeed, yes, I talked a lot in my speech about that, making sure that we have enough flexible funding which enables us to also work together with the international financial institutions and to unleash funding in sometimes circumstances where speed really is of the essence, is a big part of our work. And working together with other humanitarian players is an important one, and the cooperation with OCHA really is a crucial one. Maybe let me finish in this first round and talking also about efficiency. These were questions made by UK, Sweden, US and so on. Look, we can give you a full overview of all the cost reductions that we have done and we will continue doing so. But we also have to be clear that cost reductions cannot compensate for all the reductions in financing that we have seen. It is part of the transformation program that we do. But today, for every dollar that you give us, 91 cents is going directly into the field, which is really at the highest standards that you can expect from us. Maybe last element is in there was a question from Norway and a few others on which functions should be protected when there is a reduction in core. I think I mentioned that our country presence is a crucial one. Of course, the way core is allocated is based on a formula which is approved by the board. And so if we respect the priorities put in that formula, there is only 80 million which is left, which is based on our own discretionary decisions that we can take. So at some point, we might have to have a discussion again in this board on the allocation formula, because this allocation formula dates from a time when core was in a bigger volume. But we want to be transparent with you. In the speech, I mentioned that the current erosion of core puts 40% of the impact that we have at risk. And if that continues, it puts at risk our policy work, it puts at risk our oversight work, it puts at risk the geographical presence that we have. And we need to be aware that we will do everything to protect all those elements and we will do the transformation that is necessary to be fit for a different future. But we should all be aware that if it continues in that direction, and if you do not enable us the capacity to adapt, the impact of that could be one which is not in a far future. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Administrator. Colleagues will continue with the list of speakers. We have a significant list and we'll try to advance it as much as possible during the morning session. So we have the Netherlands, Ukraine, Australia, El Salvador, Ethiopia. I give the floor to the Netherlands. Ambassador, you have the floor, please.

Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Administrator, for your explanations. And let me start by adding my voice to those who express sympathy and condolences for the devastating -- the victims of the devastating floods in Nepal. And, of course, we condemn any attack on peacekeepers. Please allow me to make three points. First, let me underscore that the Netherlands supports UNDP's efforts to promote sustainable development, good governance, and resilience globally. We value UNDP as an important partner, both through our core and our earmarked funding. So in this context, we heard you, Mr Administrator, and we are pleased to announce that the Netherlands will provide 40 million euros in multiannual core funding to UNDP for the coming years. So predictable core funding resources are essential for UNDP to deliver effectively, maintain oversight and preserve strategic flexibility. This is particularly important given the significant decline in core contributions. And this brings me to my second point. The financial outlook requires strategic prioritization and difficult choices. UNDP has a broad mandate, but it cannot do everything everywhere. We therefore need to see greater clarity on how UNDP is adapting its program portfolio, country presence and workforce to the changing funding environment. This is important not only for efficiency, but also for UNDP's credibility as a strategic partner. A broad mandate needs to be matched by a clear sense of where UNDP can deliver the greatest added value. We see this added value in UNDP's work on governance, rule of law, conflict prevention and building resilient institutions. So we'd like to ask, where do you see the greatest scope for prioritization and what difficult choices is UNDP prepared to make to protect its core strengths? Third and finally, we welcome the ongoing UNAD reform efforts. We see a strong resident coordinator system as critical to a well-functioning UN development system and stress the importance of UNDP's active support. With UNDP engaged in 14 UNAT work packages, could you highlight where you see the greatest added value and impact for UNDP and where you see the most important opportunities to reduce duplication and improve efficiency? We expect these reforms to ultimately strengthen delivery and impact for programme countries. We also encourage UNDP and UNOPS to move forward swiftly with the agreed process on potential merger. Thank you.
I thank the Kingdom of the Netherlands for the statement. I give the floor to Ukraine, to be followed by Australia. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Mr. President, let me thank the UNDP Administrator, His Excellency, Alexander de Croo, for his strong and optimistic statement and for the continued commitment of UNDP to support countries facing complex challenges. My government highly values its partnership with UNDP. In the face of Russia's ongoing war or aggression, UNDP remains one of Ukraine's most crucial development partners, helping sustain essential services and advance recovery efforts under exceptionally difficult circumstances. Today, Ukraine especially appreciates UNDP's leadership in ensuring the resilience of national energy sector. As Russia continues its deliberate systematic attacks against Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure, maintaining access to electricity, heating, water supply remains a key priority. In this context, we are grateful for UNDP's practical and results-oriented assistance for the delivery of energy equipment, across the country. As of July 26, UNDP has procured or is procuring energy equipment with a combined capacity of more than 600 megawatts, helping communities, hospitals, schools, water utilities, and heating systems continue operating despite constant Russian intentional strikes against our infrastructure. 600 megawatts, this is roughly the yearly capacity of one of our major hydropower plants. It's just enough to give you a sense of the scale of this UNDP contribution. Mr. President, I would like to express our appreciation to the UNDP country office in Ukraine and for the dedicated UNDP team here in New York for their responsiveness and support. Your close cooperation with our authorities, local communities, and the mission has been instrumental in delivering concrete results. We're equally grateful to the donor countries whose solidarity makes all these efforts possible, the support provided by our key partners, and I will name it, Norway, Sweden, the European Union, Japan, Denmark, the Republic of Korea, Belgium, Iceland, Germany, Serbia, France, and others, they all have enabled UNDP to implement large-scale projects that improve the lives of millions of Ukrainians. We call upon other member states to join this circle of friends. To conclude, I want once again to congratulate you, dear Excellency Administrator Alexander De Croo, on your leadership and reiterate my invitation to you to visit Ukraine as soon as possible. It will offer a good opportunity to see firsthand the positive impact of UNDP work and define future priorities. I thank you.
I thank Ukraine for the statement. I give the floor to Australia, to be followed by El Salvador, and then we have Ethiopia, Thailand, Bhutan, Sri Lanka. Australia, Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you very much indeed, President. And first, let me express solidarity with Nepal at this very difficult time. Can I thank you, Administrator, very much indeed for your very clear articulation of the issues as you see them, the path towards reform, but also I think the very clear importance of core funding and us coming collectively together to have a very clear sense of where UNDP takes itself in the future. But once again, I thought your articulation was very, very helpful for us this morning. Australia, of course, remains a very strong supporter of UNDP's vital role in advancing sustainable development. I have three brief points. First, Australia welcomes the recently completed MoPAN assessment. The assessment highlights UNDP as a highly capable organization and one of the UN system's most trusted delivery partners, particularly in climate action, governance, and fragile settings. We encourage UNDP to build on these strengths while addressing the factors that can prevent strong delivery from translating into broader and more lasting development progress. We look forward to seeing this reflected in future reporting. Second, we urge UNDP to maintain momentum across practical system-wide reforms that strengthen country-level delivery and reinforce an effective resident coordinator system. As reforms progress, regional realities must remain central. This includes protecting UNDP's presence and development impact in the Pacific, where support must remain responsive to the needs of small island developing states. And I thank you very much for your response to Nauru's question earlier this morning. We stress the need for meaningful engagement with Pacific Island countries and emphasise that Member States should be consulted on significant organisational changes that may affect country presence, service delivery or development outcomes, and again very much appreciate your reaffirmation of your continued commitment to that region. Third, Australia welcomes the structured funding report and notes the continued challenges of declining regular and flexible resources. The report highlights the importance of finding a sustainable balance between organizational reform, operational effectiveness, and funding quality. We very much appreciate UNDP's efforts to improve transparency around the government local office costs plus and to address the financial pressures associated with maintaining country presence. We encourage UNDP to ensure that the unique vulnerabilities faced by SIDS are appropriately considered in cost calculations and that program countries are informed appropriately on proposed changes and implications. And we would welcome UNDP's consideration of using the multidimensional vulnerability index alongside income when calculating costs and waivers as a reflection of these unique vulnerabilities.
